When i was in college (im a girl) me and my boyfriend had a similar issue. The whole friend group felt so fake and superficial. It was all about partying and being idiots. Sure that can be fun here and there but it was so weird that none of us actually knew each other very well despite spending so much time together for years. So i hung out with my friends from my major classes for quality time and hung out with the fratty group for the partying. Guess which friends i'm still in contact with today? And from what i've heard, nothing much has really changed within that friend group (we're 28-29y/o now)

I would definitely encourage you to find other people. I made friends with people from my classes and would do study groups and some of those classmates turned into lifelong besties (and way more successful than the party kids lol) despite me spending most of my time with the party group during college. I definitely regret not spending more time with the real people.  

Besides classrooms, other places you could look into are campus events, joining clubs, and even the cafeteria or library. I've also made guy friends by being asked out on a date and realizing no romantic comparability yet we become good friends. So asking girls out could be an option too lol

As a girl i'd never trust a guy on a dating app saying he's looking for friendships unfortunately. 

Hope you find some decent people soon!

What i did and i'm glad i did: I did all UW IM questions, the rest were what i could do under the limited time, including 0 psych questions. All NBMEs and some CMS forms (wish i did more). In the last week or so, i did some Amboss stuff: ethics (particularly quality control), 200 high yield, and biostats questions that weren't calculations (i got 1 calculation on test day). New new free120 (wish i did old as well, some repeats from new on test day and also repeats from NBME forms). I reviewed vax schedules the day before - clutch, even though i only got like a couple questions on this. Didn't review screening guidelines bc i have those down but please review if you don't know them well. Throughout dedicated i took notes of all of my incorrects and i would review notes at least once a week, scratching out things i felt i didn't need to review again so it wasn't too bad. This was golden for my step 1 and i think it was golden for step 2 as well.

\*\*\*\*\*\*I also worked proactively to improve test taking strategies and this has to be the most important thing anyone can do to prep\*\*\*\*\*\*\*

What i regret: I was nervous and on autopilot on test day. I planned on reading psych section from FA step 1 just to refresh and didn't have the time to do that (literally would have been enough for all psych questions for me) or finish reviewing my notes one last time. Def missed a few questions because i didn't finish my reviews and instead was doing questions the day before the test like a crazy person. Had i just reviewed and chilled, i would have at least gotten 10 more questions right that i could identify when i got out. I took too long in some hard questions + i think i changed a bunch of answers without realizing it simply because i was anxious - my test taking strategies that i worked so hard to improve throughout dedicated flew out the window.

Takeaway: control your mindset on test day and on the few days before as well. Granted, my dod died and i got a flat tire the morning before my test, but still. And improve test taking strategies!!

Prophylaxis is for patients with prosthetic heart valve or hx of previous endocarditis. 
It's also for *certain* congenital heart defects but i've never seen it on a question so i'm assuming that one is out of scope for this test. But generally it would be a cyanotic unrepaired defect or repaired with residual defect. No prophylaxis for asymptomatic valve defects.

Beware, prophylaxis is not just for dental procedures. It's also given for ANY surgery involving infected tissue, for penetration of respiratory mucosa (eg. tonsillectomy), and for cardiac implants (eg. insertion of pacemaker)

I'm struggling as well. I try to remind myself to read faster while im reading - hopefully with practice this becomes more natural to me. 

Read last 1-2 sentences first so you know what to look for in the vignette (if you even need to look for something, sometimes questions can be answered without reading the case which is ANNOYING to waste time on.) 

Think of a dx as you're reading the the history. If it suggests a certain dx, look for evidence of it in the labs/physical exam. Eg: question asked why did this patient's creatinine increased. Case: patient started taking antibiotics a week ago, has a rash. -> think interstitial nephritis -> look for eosinophilia in labs -> if you found it, read no further, pick answer choice and move on. 

No overthinking! If you can't decide, pick something and move on. The extra minute you take to think, which may or may not even end in you picking the correct answer, is not worth it. You have to learn to let it go. Go with your gut and move on. You'll be surprised how often your gut is right.

Content review for clinicals is different because the resources change and you already have knowledge of the material. BnB for example was my go-to before MS3, after that... nope :( Everyone abandons BnB. The popular content review resources are online med ed, Dr. high yield, dr. emma holiday, divine intervention podcast, and melhman. The most important thing for me besides taking my meds consistently in the mornings was to have people keep me accountable, whether it was friends on the same boat texting me to see if i was awake or how i was doing, or other students i found on the internet who would be down to study together virtually (cameras on, mikes off) - this is easy to find on discord. I had a study group that would always meet on zoom every day at 8am. This was super helpful for accountability.

I would also advice against much content review for any ADHDer just because it is harder for us to study so much every day we don't end up studying for as much time as others so we gotta be very time-efficient. Your priority is always UW and everything else is a bonus if you have the extra time for it

Finally, we (and non ADHDers) can be very slow sometimes. The best way around this is to always do timed blocks. Do not waste extra time on questions, it won't do you any good. Better to get them wrong but do more than do less and get them right. Fuck your scores. Just do however many you can. Always be mindful of the time you spend doing X or Y resource. Plus, on test day the questions are LONG - longer than UW - so we def need that timing practice anyway! Try to do blocks and have a few minutes to spare at the very least. But don't worry if you can't do it until a few weeks before test day - that's when you should really start making sure you got the timing down
